title: Quadratic Functions and Equations
description: The discriminant, completing the square, roots, quadratic inequalities and optimisation

notes.heading: The Discriminant
notes.body:
For the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ the **discriminant** is
$$\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$$
It is the part of the quadratic formula that sits under the square root, so its sign decides how many real roots there are.

• $\Delta > 0$ — two distinct real roots.
• $\Delta = 0$ — one repeated real root (the graph touches the $x$-axis).
• $\Delta < 0$ — no real roots (the graph never meets the $x$-axis).

💡 **Worked Example** — $x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0$ has $\Delta = 16 - 4 = 12 > 0$, so there are two distinct real roots, $x = 2 \pm \sqrt{3}$.

📌 $\Delta$ is the **discriminant of an equation**, so the equation must be written with everything on one side first: for $x^2 = 3x + 5$ use $x^2 - 3x - 5 = 0$.

illustration.alt: Three parabolas against the x-axis: x² − 4 cutting it twice, x² touching it once at the origin, and x² + 4 sitting clear above it.
illustration.caption: Two crossings, one touch, no touch — the vertex in relation to the x-axis is what the discriminant is measuring.

notes.heading: Completing the Square and the Vertex
notes.body:
Writing $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ in the form
$$y = a(x-h)^2 + k$$
shows the **vertex** $(h, k)$ directly. The axis of symmetry is $x = h$.

For $a = 1$: halve the coefficient of $x$, then subtract its square. For $a \ne 1$: take the $a$ out of the first two terms first.

💡 **Worked Example** — $y = x^2 - 6x + 11$.
$$x^2 - 6x + 11 = (x-3)^2 - 9 + 11 = (x-3)^2 + 2$$
so the vertex is $(3, 2)$ and the minimum value of $y$ is 2.

💡 **Worked Example with a leading coefficient** — $y = 2x^2 + 8x + 5 = 2(x^2 + 4x) + 5 = 2\big[(x+2)^2 - 4\big] + 5 = 2(x+2)^2 - 3$, so the vertex is $(-2, -3)$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Subtracting $\dfrac{b^2}{4a}$ but forgetting to multiply it by $a$ when the bracket is expanded. Working inside the bracket, as above, avoids the error.

notes.heading: Finding the Roots
notes.body:
Three routes, in order of speed:

• **Factorising** — best when the roots are integers, e.g. $x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x-2)(x-3)$.
• **The quadratic formula** — always works:
$$x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$
• **Completing the square** — quickest when the answer is a surd and the coefficients are simple.

💡 **Worked Example** — Solve $2x^2 - 4x - 1 = 0$. Then $a = 2$, $b = -4$, $c = -1$ and $\Delta = 16 + 8 = 24$:
$$x = \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{24}}{4} = \dfrac{4 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{4} = 1 \pm \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2}$$

The **sum** of the roots is $-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and the **product** is $\dfrac{c}{a}$ — often quicker than finding the roots themselves.

📌 Give exact answers (surd form) unless the question asks for a given number of decimal places.

notes.heading: Quadratic Inequalities
notes.body:
To solve $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ or $< 0$: find the roots, then **sketch** the parabola and read off where it is above or below the $x$-axis.

For $a > 0$ (an upward parabola):
• $> 0$ outside the roots: $x < \alpha$ or $x > \beta$.
• $< 0$ between the roots: $\alpha < x < \beta$.

💡 **Worked Example** — Solve $x^2 - x - 6 > 0$.
Factorising gives $(x-3)(x+2) > 0$, so the roots are $-2$ and $3$. The parabola opens upwards, so it is above the axis outside the roots:
$$x < -2 \quad \text{or} \quad x > 3$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Writing the answer as $-2 > x > 3$, which is empty, or copying the "between the roots" answer when the inequality sign asks for outside. Sketching takes five seconds and removes the ambiguity.

📌 If $a < 0$, multiply through by $-1$ and **reverse the inequality sign**, or sketch the downward parabola.

notes.heading: Using the Discriminant as a Condition
notes.body:
Many exam questions hand you a property (equal roots, tangency, no real roots) and ask for an unknown constant. The method is always the same: form a quadratic, then impose the right condition on $\Delta$.

💡 **Worked Example** — Find $k$ so that $x^2 + kx + 9 = 0$ has equal roots.
$$\Delta = k^2 - 36 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; k = \pm 6$$

💡 **Tangency** — Find $c$ so that $y = 3x + c$ is tangent to $y = x^2 + x + 5$.
Setting the two expressions equal: $x^2 + x + 5 = 3x + c$, so $x^2 - 2x + (5 - c) = 0$. Tangency means exactly one intersection, so $\Delta = 0$:
$$4 - 4(5 - c) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; c = 4$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Forgetting that $k = \pm 6$ is two answers; a square root of a positive number is never one-signed.

notes.heading: Graph Features and Symmetry
notes.body:
Every parabola is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex. If the roots are $p$ and $q$, then the axis of symmetry is
$$x = \dfrac{p + q}{2}$$
which is also the average of any two points with the same $y$-coordinate.

**Sketching checklist** — the sign of $a$ (upward if $a > 0$, downward if $a < 0$); the $y$-intercept at $(0, c)$; the roots from $y = a(x-p)(x-q)$; and the vertex, which sits at the midpoint of the roots.

💡 **Worked Example** — For $y = x^2 - 8x + 12$ the roots are 2 and 6, so the axis of symmetry is $x = 4$ and the vertex is $(4, 16 - 32 + 12) = (4, -4)$.

🔑 Symmetry in symbols: $f(h + t) = f(h - t)$ for every $t$, where $h$ is the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. That identity is the quickest proof that a curve is symmetric about $x = h$.

notes.heading: Quadratic Optimisation and Exam Technique
notes.body:
A quadratic has a single maximum or minimum, at its vertex — which is why quadratic models answer "largest area" and "greatest profit" questions.

💡 **Worked Example** — A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm. Find the maximum area.
Let one side be $x$; the other is $12 - x$. Then
$$A = x(12 - x) = -(x - 6)^2 + 36$$
so the largest possible area is 36 cm², when the rectangle is a 6 cm by 6 cm square.

**Exam technique**
• Build the expression in one variable before optimising; write down what the other variable is in terms of it.
• Complete the square or use $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$ to locate the vertex, then substitute to find the extreme value.
• Answer the question that was asked: the value of $x$ *and* the maximum, if both are wanted.

⚠️ **Common mistakes** — Giving the $x$-coordinate of the vertex as the maximum value; ignoring a practical restriction such as a positive side length; and rounding an exact surd value too early.

questions.stem: A quadratic equation has discriminant $\Delta < 0$. How many real roots does it have?
questions.explanation: A negative discriminant makes the square root in the quadratic formula undefined over the reals, so the equation has no real roots.

questions.stem: State the vertex of the graph of $y = (x-3)^2 + 4$.
questions.explanation: Vertex form $y = (x-h)^2 + k$ has vertex $(h, k)$, so here it is $(3, 4)$.

questions.stem: Find the axis of symmetry of the graph of $y = x^2 - 8x + 1$.
questions.explanation: Completing the square gives $y = (x-4)^2 - 15$, so the axis of symmetry is $x = 4$. The formula $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = \dfrac{8}{2}$ gives the same value.

questions.stem: How many real roots does $2x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0$ have?
questions.explanation: $\Delta = (-4)^2 - 4(2)(3) = 16 - 24 = -8 < 0$, so the equation has no real roots.

questions.stem: Find the sum of the roots of $3x^2 - 12x + 7 = 0$.
questions.explanation: The sum of the roots is $-\dfrac{b}{a} = -\dfrac{-12}{3} = 4$.
$(x-5)(x+1) < 0$ has roots $-1$ and 5. The parabola opens upwards, so it is below the $x$-axis between the roots: $-1 < x < 5$.

questions.stem: Find all values of $k$ for which $x^2 + kx + 16 = 0$ has equal roots.
questions.explanation: Equal roots need $\Delta = k^2 - 64 = 0$, so $k^2 = 64$ and $k = \pm 8$.
Completing the square: $2x^2 - 8x + 11 = 2(x-2)^2 + 3$. Since a square is never negative, the minimum is 3 (at $x = 2$).

questions.stem: The line $y = 3x + c$ is tangent to the curve $y = x^2 + x + 5$. Find $c$.
questions.explanation: Equating gives $x^2 + x + 5 = 3x + c$, so $x^2 - 2x + (5 - c) = 0$. Tangency means one repeated root, so $\Delta = 4 - 4(5-c) = 0$, giving $4c = 16$ and $c = 4$.

questions.stem: Find the product of the roots of $2x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0$.
questions.explanation: The product of the roots is $\dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{-3}{2} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$.

questions.stem: A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm. Find the largest possible area of the rectangle.
questions.explanation: If one side is $x$ cm the other is $(12 - x)$ cm, so $A = x(12-x) = -(x-6)^2 + 36$. The maximum area is $36 \text{ cm}^2$, when the rectangle is a square of side 6 cm.

questions.stem: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^2 + 2x + (3 - k) = 0$ has two distinct real roots.
